story_text.value:
Memcode is a new developer platform currently in public beta. It includes a coding agent, chat, reusable agents, DataHub, and a Lovable-style website generator.

The coding agent is heavily inspired by Claude Code and works across all frontier models as well as open-weight models such as Kimi and GLM.

Memcode was designed to stay in sync with you and behave more like a human coworker, with persistent memory and state recall. It grew out of constant frustration with existing coding agents.

If your current coding agent already works great for you, Memcode may not be especially compelling. But if you regularly find yourself repeating context, correcting lost assumptions, or fighting to keep an agent on track, or you simply enjoy trying new developer tools, give Memcode a try.

https://memcode.ai

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I’ve had a goal on my mind for a while: to automate the process of figuring out what people actually want.

I’m building a set of tools to find app concepts worth building and niches that are overlooked or badly served.

The first piece is Seam. It connects to Google Play and can read thousands of recent reviews for any app, then pull out the main complaints and pain points. The idea is to help you figure out exactly what to build if you want to compete with an existing app or address the same niche.

You can ask it to aggregate the complaints and strengths across a bunch of similar apps too. This makes it useful for analyzing competitors, or even your own published app, although, to be honest, that wasn’t my original goal.

It’s completely free for now. You get 3 messages without an account and 30 free messages if you create one.

I’ve started exploring a few related ideas as well. One is analyzing social media posts, basically looking for people asking things like “How can I do X?” or “Is there a tool for X?” and finding recurring pain points.

Another is automating demo video creation to see which concepts get the most engagement on social media, also trying to look at past Product Hunt and Indie Hackers submissions to help predict which concepts are likely to succeed too. Adding support for Trustpilot and the App Store is on my list as well.

I think combining all of these data sources could be really useful for systematically finding concepts to build that people already want.

I’d love some feedback on the overall concept and to know whether I’m the only one interested in this kind of tool before investing more time in it.

Thanks!

story_text.value:
Over this past weekend I built a web app called Blink Ideas.

It finds customer complaints and feedback on places like HN, StackExchange, app store reviews, and more.

Then it generates real startup solutions, scored with their investment opportunity based risk, market appeal, scalability, and other major factors.

It provides a solution, MVP, and even competitor list to help you gain insights before building.

Now more than ever, starting a business or building an app is the easy part. Creating something that makes money that people actually want is the hard part.

That's why I built this app.

It makes starting your next side project or startup a piece of cake, saving weeks or months of research and helping you build something people actually use.

It makes building worth your while and will deliver you a return on your time and effort.

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I and my co founder built Mint MCP, a remote server that lets Codex, Claude Code, and Cursor create 3D models, worlds, materials, images, and audio.

The server handles long-running jobs, preview revisions, partial failures, and file delivery. When generation finishes, Mint gives the agent stable links to the files and tells it what each file is for, so it can add them to the project.

You can try it at mcp.mint.gg. It requires a Mint subscription but msg me and i can set you up with some free credits!

I’d like feedback from anyone using coding agents for 3D or asset-heavy projects. We have a massive repo of open source templates for you to use/play around with on play.mint.gg

story_text.value:
I wrote libcorrect in C in 2016 and wanted to revisit it in Rust. Instead of doing just a direct conversion, I went down the rabbit hole of making Rust's std::simd work for me. I ended up with a templated, generic Viterbi decoder for convolutional codes that dispatches the decode at runtime depending on which instruction sets are available. For small rates and orders, the entire decode lives in registers. Larger codes work through memory but take advantage of some acceleration structures.

I also spent some time building a tool to find optimal (max d_free) conv codes for a given rate and order. Of course, there are better mechanisms available today, but I'm happy to talk through anything I learned in the process.

title.value: Show HN: SIMD Viterbi Decoder in Rust

story_text.value:
There are a number of AI benchmarks but I feel they aren't practical when it comes to evaluating AI products. Several months back we started working on designing a methodology to independently evaluate AI products. After conducting a good bit of research, we tested the methodology on a few different categories of products and improvised it. 
If this is an area of interest to you, may I request you to review this methodology and help us with feedback. A quick blurb on the structure of the methodology - It's a 3-tier framework starting with 6 high level evaluation categories (Quality, Security, Privacy & safety, Use cases & pricing, Sustainability & ecosystem, and Impact & ethics). 
The methodology is available at huby.ai/methodology.
Thanks in advance.

story_text.value:
TLDR: Collab WIW is a DOCX editor with MS Word parity that supports real-time collaborative editing between humans and BYO Agents.

The collab layer is end to end encrypted and uses ephemeral rooms with stable share URLs. Ever collab room lives in only memory. Collaborator saved copies can bring the room back online at the same URL and reconcile offline edits.

For BYO Agents, you generate an invite link into Codex or Claude. The AI runs the linked WordInWeb agent package, connects to the document, and opens up a private chat in the browser with the user who invited the agent. Everyone sees its document activity, but only the inviter can chat with and direct it.

The MS Word parity DOCX editor: I made a previous HN post about the editor itself. It is a pure JS DOCX editor that renders and edits the original document directly in the DOM instead of converting it into some other format.

I benchmarked it pretty heavily against thousands of pages to push for pixel and feature parity, including equations, tables, 3D objects, headers, footnotes, etc... I am not going to get too deep into that because I already posted a ShowHN earlier. The parity report has all of the fixtures I tested and the actual results.

Edit: Link to previous HN https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48995304

The server: The collab BE was actually inspired by OpenFront.io :). Users send small edit intents to the server. In an encrypted room the server cannot process those edits because it cannot read them. It just gives each encrypted envelope the next sequence number and sends the same ordered stream to everybody in the room.

Collaborative rooms: The rooms are ephemeral and the server keeps their encrypted document state in memory. I chose these constraints because this is a public demo. I wanted people to create and share a document ad-hoc without making an account. I also don't your data plz, no thank you.

Also because intents are tracked by document there is some support offline editing support and document reconciliation when it comes back up. Its still a bit ugly so there are limits, if the document can't be cleanly fast forwarded, the editor will try to reconcile up to 50 intents. If there are no conflicts the document fast forward to 2000 tailing intents. After that point you just gotta create a new draft. Just cleaner that way. I am still actively working on improving this system and figuring out how it can be improved.

E2EE:

1. Documents, edits, images, cursor positions, etc... are encrypted in your browser and stay encrypted on the server. The document key is generated in the browser and lives in the share link's fragment, and never gets sent to the server. The server just sequences the sealed data.

2. A document also requires require a share code that you send separately from the link. The browser stretches that code and mixes it into key derivation, so the link by itself is not enough to decrypt the room.

4. Resource limits are placed basically everywhere.

Blog covers more details.

title.value: Show HN: Collab Word in Web – Collaborative Near MS Word Parity Docx Editor

story_text.value:
Hi!

I have relatives that speak sign language, and always found it odd that despite unbelievable advances in AI in recent years, the problem still felt somewhat neglected.

Especially with the advent of wearable tech; to my knowledge, this is the first project that integrates the meta glasses w/ fingerspelling translation software.

As for the technical aspect, I trained a neural net on Google's FSboard dataset modeling a CNN + GRU temporal encoder architecture (trained with CTC), and then decoded the output with CTC beam search and a KenLM language model to solve some of the deficiencies with my model.

I've also made it cross-platform (web + iOS, with both web screen sharing and the ability to use non smart-glasses). The project is entirely FOSS.

I'm currently working on making the on-device model work cleanly, but unfortunately performance takes a bit of hit on lower-end devices so for now I've opted for hosting the model on Modal.

There's so much room for improvement, but I'm happy with this starting point. Let me know what you think, and check out the YouTube demo!
